transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I keep rechecking and fixing how I look before I go out or get on camera, and it’s starting to make me late and stressed all the time. It is just getting really hard to manage, and I feel like I need some help figuring out how to stop this cycle.
Do you feel compelled to recheck your appearance because of persistent, intrusive thoughts that something is wrong, even if you know it might not make sense?

Yes, I really do. I can't stop obsessing over my jaw looking crooked and my skin looking bad, even though my friends insist they don't see anything wrong. I get completely stuck in front of the mirror adjusting my hair, changing clothes, and taking test selfies over and over just to feel "less ugly" before I can leave.
Have these concerns about your appearance and the need to check them been ongoing for more than six months, or do they come and go with changes in your mood or stress levels?

Yes, they've been ongoing and persistent ever since I started college and began dating, which was over a year ago. It's been a constant, daily struggle ever since those teasing comments about my photo, rather than something that just comes and goes with my mood.
When you're checking your appearance, do you feel like these flaws are actually noticeable to others, or do you understand that they might be mostly in your mind?

To be honest, it feels incredibly real and noticeable to me, and I can't help but zoom in on my crooked jaw and bad skin in every picture. Even though my friends insist they don't see anything wrong or weird at all, I just can't shake the feeling that it's completely obvious to everyone.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F42", "F34.1"], but based on this conversation, F34.1 (persistent mood disorder) seems unlikely because the patient reports that the symptoms are persistent and not fluctuating with mood changes. The patient describes intrusive, distressing preoccupations with perceived appearance flaws (e.g., crooked jaw, bad skin), engages in repetitive checking behaviors (mirror use, selfies), recognizes some discrepancy with others' perceptions, and has had daily, unremitting symptoms for over a year—features most consistent with an obsessive-compulsive related disorder. The chronicity, ego-dystonic nature, and compulsive rituals strongly support F42 (obsessive-compulsive disorder), particularly with somatic concerns. No features suggest an enduring mild mood disturbance as primary, ruling out F34.1. Therefore, the current candidate is solely F42.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent and intrusive preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance (jaw crookedness, skin quality) that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive checking behaviors (mirror use, selfies) aimed at reducing distress. Symptoms have been present for over six months with significant functional impairment, consistent with body dysmorphic disorder.
